knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 26-year-old male with no known health issues presented with purulent discharge from the umbilicus and intermittent umbilical pain for the past month. The patient also reported recent onset of burning sensation during urination. Physical examination revealed a hirsute male with a deep, erythematous umbilicus exhibiting purulent discharge. Urinalysis results were unremarkable.. Confirmed diagnosis: Urachal Sinus. Differential diagnosis includes: Urachal Sinus.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Urachal Sinus

knowledge_fragments.content:
Common symptoms and signs
Adults with acute sinusitis usually present with:
nasal blockage or congestion
nasal discharge
dental or facial pain or pressure
reduction or loss of the sense of smell.
Children (particularly young children) often present with non‑specific symptoms in the upper respiratory tract. Symptoms of acute sinusitis in children may include the following, but these can be present for many upper respiratory tract infections:
nasal blockage or congestion
discoloured nasal discharge
cough during the day or at night.
knowledge_fragments.title: Symptoms and signs > Symptoms and signs > Common symptoms and signs

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 40-year-old male presented with a 10-month history of watery nasal discharge. He also reported a history of headaches and nasal obstruction, previously attributed to hypertrophied turbinate, for which surgery was recommended but declined. Over the past 2 years, the patient experienced a gradual onset of anosmia, initially without watery discharge but associated with nasal obstruction. The watery nasal discharge increased when bending forward or coughing and trickled into the nasopharynx without any detectable taste. This discharge was also associated with headaches. The patient has no history of nasal trauma, surgery, or signs of meningitis.. Confirmed diagnosis: Spontaneous Lateral Intrasphenoidal Encephalocele. Differential diagnosis includes: Spontaneous Lateral Intrasphenoidal Encephalocele.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Spontaneous Lateral Intrasphenoidal Encephalocele

knowledge_fragments.content: ❖ Nasal chondritis is less symptomatic and more common, with a prevalence of 60% cases, and is characterized by inflammation of the nasal cartilage, with symptoms of pain, nasal discharge, or obstruction. A deformity of the nasal bridge may be observed over time, known as “saddle nose”. This deformity can be seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), which is usually preceded by more pronounced symptoms.
knowledge_fragments.title: Relapsing polychondritis: tracheobronchial involvement and differential diagnoses. > Clinical manifestations > Other clinical manifestations

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 40-year-old female presented to our center in April 2010 with complaints of left breast pain and purulent discharge. She reported no recent pregnancy, lactation, or breast trauma. She had first noticed a painful mass in her left breast one year prior, and in the last 20 days, she observed a visible skin lesion on the breast with purulent discharge. There was no history of previous antibiotic therapy for tuberculosis, family history of tuberculosis, diabetes mellitus, weight loss, or fever. She had undergone at least three courses of antibiotic therapy prescribed by a local physician without any improvement. Physical examination revealed a painful nodular mass near the nipple of the left breast, accompanied by a discharging sinus.. Confirmed diagnosis: Breast Tuberculosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Breast Tuberculosis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Breast Tuberculosis

knowledge_fragments.content: The presence of unilateral symptoms, isolated nasal obstruction, mucopurulent rhinorrhea, posterior nasal discharge with viscous mucus with/without anterior rhinorrhea, pain, epistaxis, and isolated anosmia should direct the differential diagnosis to other clinical entities. For instance, chronic mucopurulent rhinitis may suggest the presence of rhinosinusitis due to adenoid hypertrophy, anatomical anomalies, primary immunodeficiency, primary ciliary dyskinesia, or cystic fibrosis.
knowledge_fragments.title: A Clinical Approach of Allergic Rhinitis in Children. > 2. Diagnosis

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 73-year-old female presented with a 2-month history of continuous clear nasal discharge, which had been previously managed as rhinitis by a pulmonologist, and was subsequently referred to the ear–nose–throat (ENT) department. Physical examination showed right-sided nasal discharge. There was no history of head trauma or cranial surgery. The nasal discharge was identified as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea.. Confirmed diagnosis: Encephalocele within the lateral recess of the sphenoid sinus due to persistence of Sternberg's canal. Differential diagnosis includes: Encephalocele within the lateral recess of the sphenoid sinus due to persistence of Sternberg's canal.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Encephalocele within the lateral recess of the sphenoid sinus due to persistence of Sternberg's canal

knowledge_fragments.content: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.
knowledge_fragments.title: Cranial Autonomic Symptoms and Neck Pain in Differential Diagnosis of Migraine. > 2. Cranial Autonomic Symptoms > 2.3. CAS in Other Headaches and Differential Diagnosis

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 41-year-old woman visited the ENT clinic in January 2020 with clear to yellowish nasal discharge from the right nostril. The nasal discharge began 2 months after her cesarean section delivery. During the physical examination, inflammation of the nasal vestibule was observed, for which she was prescribed antibiotics (Augmentin) for 1 week, resulting in significant symptom improvement. Five months later, she returned with a 2-week history of brownish-to-greenish nasal discharge. She was treated again with Augmentin, nasal hypertonic saline, and mometasone furate sprays.. Confirmed diagnosis: Actinomycosis of the paranasal sinuses. Differential diagnosis includes: Actinomycosis of the paranasal sinuses.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Actinomycosis of the paranasal sinuses

History: History of present illness

should ascertain how long swelling has been present, whether it is

unilateral or bilateral, and whether it has been preceded by any trauma (including insect bites). Important

accompanying symptoms to identify include itching, pain, headache, change in vision, fever, and eye

discharge.

Review of systems

should seek symptoms of possible causes, including runny nose, itching, rash, and

wheezing (systemic allergic reaction); headache, nasal congestion, and purulent nasal discharge

failure); cold intolerance and changes in skin texture (hypothyroidism); and heat intolerance, anxiety, and

weight loss (hyperthyroidism).

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 42-year-old Caucasian woman presented with severe right-sided ear pain and purulent discharge for 45 days, unresponsive to multiple antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, ciprofloxacin, and ceftriaxone) and systemic and topical steroids. She subsequently developed vertigo, headache, and severe mixed hearing loss on the right side. Her medical history included renal dysfunction of unknown cause and a kidney-transplanted sister. Physical examination revealed a central perforation of the right tympanic membrane with a visible red mass resembling a polyp and purulent discharge. Other ENT examinations were normal. Laboratory tests showed purulent discharge with pneumococcus sensitive to the antibiotics used, neutrophilia with a left shift in the CBC, elevated ESR, and proteinuria. Imaging studies included a temporal bone CT scan showing blurring of the tympanic cavity and mastoid cells, and a skull MRI revealing a hyperintense signal in T2 on the right mastoid bone. Due to lack of clinical improvement, tympanomastoidectomy was performed, along with the placement of a ventilation tube on the right side to address the inflammatory process and collect material. A history of recurrent abscess followed by intermittent or constant discharge is usual. Discharge material

is purulent, serosanguineous, or both. Pain may be present if there is infection. On inspection, one or

more secondary openings can be seen. A cordlike tract can often be palpated. A probe inserted into the

tract can determine the depth and direction and often the primary opening.
